a: A bank vault where the same key locks and unlocks the door — fast, sturdy, and only as safe as whoever holds that one key.
e: AES is the cipher itself; the others are modes or protocols that use it.

a: A mailbox with a public slot anyone can drop letters into, but only the owner's private key opens the back door.
e: RSA handles key exchange and signing; TLS is the protocol built around it.

a: A tiny padlock forged from much harder steel — a 256-bit ECC key guards as well as a 3072-bit RSA brick.
e: ECC gets RSA-level strength from much smaller keys, ideal for mobile and IoT.

a: The whole passport system — the issuing office, the photo ID, the border check, and the list of stolen passports.
e: PKI is the entire trust system; CA, CRL and OCSP are its parts.

a: The passport office: you trust a stranger's ID only because a government you trust stamped it.
e: The CA is the trusted signer; the rest are formats and status checks.

a: A bouncer's printed list of banned IDs — reliable, but only as current as the last time it was printed.
e: A CRL is a periodic downloadable list; OCSP answers per certificate in real time.

a: Phoning the bank at checkout to ask whether this one card is still valid, instead of reading last week's list.
e: OCSP checks one certificate live; a CRL is a bulk list downloaded periodically.

a: A fingerprint scanner for data — change a single comma and the fingerprint comes out completely different.
e: SHA proves data unchanged, but without a key it cannot prove who sent it.

a: A wax seal pressed with a stamp only you and the recipient own — it proves the letter is untouched and came from you.
e: HMAC adds a shared secret to a hash, giving integrity plus authenticity.

a: A tamper-evident envelope that both hides the letter and shows if anyone opened it.
e: GCM encrypts and authenticates in one pass, unlike plain counter mode.

a: A numbered ticket roll: each ticket number is encrypted into a one-time pad and XORed with your data.
e: Counter mode encrypts but does not authenticate; GCM adds the authentication.

a: A shipping envelope with a clear 'BEGIN CERTIFICATE' label — the box format, not the contents' security.
e: PEM is only a text encoding format; it provides no security on its own.

a: Swapping a good padlock on the Wi-Fi door for a modern one that also flags tampering.
e: GCMP is GCM applied to Wi-Fi frames in WPA3, replacing WPA2's CCMP.

a: Translating a book word by word with a fixed dictionary — every repeated word looks identical, so patterns shine through.
e: ECB encrypts identical blocks identically, leaking patterns; never use it for data.

a: A daisy chain where each link is twisted by the one before it, so identical links never look the same.
e: CBC hides patterns that ECB leaks, but needs a random IV and is sequential.

a: A cipher used like a dripping tap: it feeds back its own output to encrypt a stream bit by bit.
e: CFB turns a block cipher into a stream cipher that recovers from lost bits.

a: Shuffling the deck before every game, so the same hand never deals out the same way twice.
e: An IV is not secret, but it must never repeat with the same key.

a: A tiny safe welded onto the motherboard that holds keys and remembers exactly how the computer booted.
e: A TPM is built into one device; an HSM is a dedicated enterprise appliance.

a: The free, open-source edition of the same sealed-envelope service PGP sells.
e: GPG implements the OpenPGP standard freely; PGP was the original product.

a: Sealing a letter with the recipient's padlock and signing it with your personal wax stamp.
e: PGP uses a web of trust between users instead of central certificate authorities.

a: Two diplomats meeting first to agree on a secret language before any real messages are sent.
e: IKE only negotiates keys and SAs; IPSec then protects the actual traffic.

a: A notary stamp: it proves who signed a document but never hides what the document says.
e: DSA only signs; unlike RSA it cannot be used to encrypt data.

a: Burning each day's codebook at sunset, so a key stolen tomorrow can't unlock yesterday's mail.
e: PFS uses ephemeral keys, so stealing the server key can't decrypt past sessions.

a: Tuning a biometric door until it wrongly lets in strangers exactly as often as it wrongly locks out staff.
e: CER is where FAR equals FRR; a lower CER means a more accurate system.

a: The same balance point as CER, just under its other name, like 'soda' and 'pop'.
e: EER and CER are the same thing: where false accepts equal false rejects.

a: An armored bank vault for keys — the keys are used inside it and never leave.
e: An HSM is a dedicated, tamper-resistant appliance, unlike a TPM built into one device.

a: A sealed pneumatic tube between your browser and the server: anyone can see the tube, nobody can read the capsule.
e: TLS is the protocol; AES, RSA and PKI are the building blocks inside it.

a: Ordinary web mail, but sent in a locked armored truck instead of on a postcard.
e: HTTPS is just HTTP wrapped in TLS on port 443.

a: A private, soundproof phone line to a remote server's command prompt.
e: SSH is the secure tunnel on port 22; SCP and SFTP move files through it.

a: The postal trucks moving letters between post offices — by default the letters are postcards anyone can read.
e: Plain SMTP on port 25 is cleartext; SMTPS or STARTTLS adds encryption.

a: Sitting at a computer across the world through a window — great for admins, a magnet for attackers if left open.
e: RDP on 3389 should never face the internet; put it behind a VPN or gateway.

a: A private underground tunnel running beneath a crowded public road.
e: A VPN is the tunnel concept; IPSec and TLS are protocols that build it.

a: Armoring every individual package at the shipping dock, no matter which app packed it.
e: IPSec secures every IP packet at Layer 3, unlike TLS which secures one application.

a: A security camera with an alarm — it sees the burglar and shouts, but doesn't lock the door.
e: An IDS is passive and only alerts; an IPS sits inline and blocks.

a: A security guard standing in the doorway who physically stops anyone suspicious.
e: An IPS sits inline and blocks traffic; a false positive can block legitimate users.

a: A bouncer who reads every web request word by word and turns away the ones carrying SQL or script tricks.
e: A WAF understands HTTP itself, unlike a network firewall that sees only IPs and ports.

a: Painting colored lanes on one shared floor so each department's traffic stays in its own lane.
e: A VLAN splits one physical switch into isolated broadcast domains.

a: The hallways inside one building — everyone nearby, connected without leaving the premises.
e: A LAN covers one site; MAN covers a city and WAN spans regions.

a: The highway system connecting cities — the internet is the biggest highway network of all.
e: A WAN links distant sites, usually over carrier or internet connections.

a: The same office hallways, but you walk them through the air instead of along cables.
e: A WLAN is a LAN over 802.11 radio, so it needs WPA2 or WPA3 protection.

a: A city's subway system — bigger than one building, smaller than the national railway.
e: A MAN sits between LAN and WAN, covering a campus or city.

a: The invisible bubble around you where your phone, earbuds and watch talk to each other.
e: A PAN covers a few meters around one person, typically Bluetooth or NFC.

a: A border checkpoint that checks every vehicle's papers against a rulebook before letting it through.
e: A basic firewall filters by IP, port and protocol; an NGFW also understands applications.

a: A notarized phone book, where every entry carries a signature proving nobody forged the number.
e: DNSSEC proves DNS answers are authentic but does not encrypt them.
m: Domain Names Signed Securely Each Certificate

a: A phone book that updates itself whenever you move to a new apartment.
e: DDNS keeps a name pointing at an IP that changes, often after DHCP renewals.
